title: Anisotropic Friedel oscillations and isoperimetric transport in two-dimensional free lattice Fermi seas
abstract: Two physical consequences of the recent topological classification of 2d Fermi seas for free particles based on flat orbifolds $\mathbb{R}^2/Γ$ of discrete symmetry $Γ$, are explored. The first is an study of the spatial density behavior inside the mesoscopic window enclosed by the Fermi and (infinite) thermal lengths. It is shown that the single-particle density matrix exhibits a sharp directional anisotropy, encoding a real space diffraction pattern, {\it i.e.}, a Fraunhofer-like diagram of the Fermi sea, that reveals the point-group symmetries of the background lattice $Γ$ in the form of anisotropic Friedel oscillations. As examples, the special cases of the $p4m$ and $p6m$ crystallographic flat orbifolds are treated in some detail. The second physical consequence is the establishment of an explicit geometric correspondence between momentum-space packing and electrical transport. A mean-field expression for the longitudinal electrical conductivity $σ_{xx}$ as a function of the {\it isoperimetric parameter} $\cal{I}$ of the occupied orbifold domain by utilizing geometric measure theory is presented, satisfiying the scaling law $ σ_{xx} \propto 1/\sqrt{\cal{I}}$. The topological transport formula naturally incorporates the vanishing conductivity ($σ_{xx} \to 0$) of the previously described ``geometric insulators,'' promoting the isoperimetric parameter as an efficient descriptor for topological and geometric phases in conductors.
summary: This theoretical work investigates how underlying lattice symmetries constrain the physics of 2D free electron gases, leading to anisotropic density patterns. It derives a universal relationship showing that electrical conductivity scales inversely with the square root of the Fermi surface's isoperimetric parameter. This framework unifies geometric topology, density oscillations, and transport properties into a single, powerful descriptor.
main_problem: The paper explores the physical consequences of classifying 2D Fermi seas using flat orbifolds defined by discrete lattice symmetries ($\Gamma$). It connects the geometry of the Fermi surface to measurable quantities like density modulations and electrical conductivity.
main_result: It establishes that the single-particle density matrix exhibits anisotropic Friedel oscillations dictated by lattice symmetry, and it derives a universal scaling law for conductivity: $\sigma_{xx} \propto 1/\sqrt{\mathcal{I}}$, where $\mathcal{I}$ is the isoperimetric parameter.
method: The analysis combines concepts from geometric measure theory, chiral anomaly calculations (bosonization), and the study of single-particle density matrices on orbifold manifolds.
model_or_system: The system is a non-interacting 2D free gas of fermions confined to a background with discrete lattice symmetries, modeled mathematically as a flat orbifold $\mathbb{R}^2/\Gamma$. The analysis covers both the density structure and the resulting macroscopic transport properties.
key_observables: Anisotropic Friedel oscillations in the single-particle density matrix, and the longitudinal electrical conductivity ($\sigma_{xx}$).
important_parameters: The isoperimetric parameter ($\mathcal{I}$), Fermi wavelength ($\lambda_F$), and thermal de Broglie wavelength ($\lambda_T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a mean-field approach for conductivity and assumes that the topological structure dictates the universal scaling laws, even when incorporating structural drag from orbifold corners.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spatial density matrix $ho(\mathbf{r}, 0)$ for specific lattices ($p4m, p6m$), showing anisotropic diffraction patterns, and reference power-law decay regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing the isotropic case (ideal 2D gas) to the anisotropic case using flat orbifolds. It then develops the conductivity calculation by relating the Fermi surface geometry to the isoperimetric parameter, culminating in a unified formula incorporating structural drag from orbifold corners.
why_interesting: The work provides a powerful geometric descriptor ($\mathcal{I}$) to unify mesoscopic density physics (Friedel oscillations) with macroscopic transport (conductivity) in a way that transcends simple continuum models, suggesting new topological invariants for conductors.
